summary:
Perak stands under Malaysia's national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency" with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysians and reach visitors; sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Every Malaysian state, Perak included, maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", carrying up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only. Enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, while the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented national pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, so a visitor's documents will be read as issued, and discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable.
tangentialFactors:
Human Dignity Trust's Malaysia country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records a crackdown under way since the 2018 general election. An October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur produced arrests of at least 20 LGBT people; an August raid on an LGBT venue in the same city saw twenty men arrested; a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned; and in November 2023 Johor state authorities announced plans for conversion-therapy centres.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, in a report released on 10 August 2022 titled "I Don't Want to Change Myself — Anti-LGBT Conversion Practices, Discrimination, and Violence in Malaysia", interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021. The report documents the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and government-run "rehabilitation" programmes that at least 1,733 people had attended as of June 2021.

The inventory names no enforcement case inside Perak itself. The national crackdown framework governs what a visitor faces here, and the dated incidents above are drawn from other states and the federal territories rather than from Perak.
localsOnly:
Perak's Sharia enactment binds Muslim residents and Muslim visitors only, and is enforced by the state Islamic religious department rather than the police. The offence of cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman" carries up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, and the text of the enactment supplies no legal definition of transgender dressing, leaving the threshold to enforcement discretion.

Malaysia records no legal procedure by which a person can change their recognised gender, so identity documents, religious registration and civil status remain fixed at birth assignment for residents of Perak as elsewhere.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees by June 2021, per the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report, which drew on interviews with 73 LGBT people conducted between 2018 and 2021. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported nationally, and transgender people are identified as particularly vulnerable.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Perak-specific enforcement case appears in the source inventory; the raid, caning and conversion-therapy incidents cited here occurred in Kuala Lumpur, Terengganu and Johor. Whether Perak has enacted provisions beyond the standard cross-dressing offence, and how often its religious department acts, is unresolved on the available sources.

The Human Dignity Trust profile was last updated on 16 December 2025 and speaks to Malaysia nationally; the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters fieldwork covers 2018 to 2021 and is not refreshed beyond that window. Whether the federal crackdown reported since 2018 has produced arrests in Perak is not sourced either way.
